BRIEF AND ARGUMENT FOR PLAINTIFF-APPELLANT

No. 1-23-1456
IN THE APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS
FIRST JUDICIAL DISTRICT
PRIYA RAMAN, Plaintiff-Appellant,
v.
SUMMIT ASCENT CLIMBING, LLC, Defendant-Appellee.
Appeal from the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, Law Division, No. 2022 L 004512, The Honorable Margaret A. Doyle, Judge Presiding

NATURE OF THE CASE

Priya Raman was badly hurt when an automatic belay device at a climbing gym run by Summit Ascent Climbing, LLC, failed to catch her. (C. 12-14.) She sued for negligence and for willful and wanton conduct. (C. 9-18.) The circuit court dismissed both counts under section 2-619(a)(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure, holding that a release in her membership agreement barred them. (C. 141; R. 22.) Raman appeals from that judgment. No question is raised on the pleadings.

ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW

1. Whether a release of injuries arising from “the inherent risks of climbing” bars a claim that the gym failed to maintain the equipment meant to protect climbers from those risks.

2. Whether a release can bar a claim for willful and wanton conduct.

JURISDICTION

The circuit court dismissed the complaint with prejudice on August 9, 2023. (C. 141.) Raman filed her notice of appeal on September 6, 2023. (C. 144.) This Court has jurisdiction over an appeal from a final judgment. Ill. S. Ct. R. 301 (eff. Feb. 1, 1994); Ill. S. Ct. R. 303 (eff. July 1, 2017).

STATUTE INVOLVED

Section 2-619(a)(9) of the Code of Civil Procedure provides:

“Defendant may, within the time for pleading, file a motion for dismissal of the action * * * [if] the claim asserted against defendant is barred by other affirmative matter avoiding the legal effect of or defeating the claim.” 735 ILCS 5/2-619(a)(9) (West 2022).

STATEMENT OF FACTS

Summit Ascent runs an indoor climbing gym in Chicago. (Compl. ¶ 4.) When Raman joined in January 2021, she signed a two-page membership agreement. (Compl. Ex. A, at 1-2.) Its release covers “any injury arising from the inherent risks of climbing, including falls,” and says nothing about the gym’s equipment or its upkeep. (Id. at 2.)

On March 14, 2022, Raman was climbing a wall served by an auto-belay device, which lowers a climber who lets go. (Compl. ¶¶ 9–10.) The device’s cable had frayed, and the gym’s inspection log shows that no one had checked it in eleven weeks, though the maker calls for a check every day. (Compl. ¶¶ 11–13; C. 61.) When Raman let go at the top of the wall, the cable failed, and she fell about 30 feet to the floor. (Compl. ¶ 14.) She broke her pelvis and her left wrist. (Compl. ¶ 15.) A gym employee testified that the manager had told staff to skip the daily checks to save time. (Ortiz Dep. 31:4-19.)

Summit Ascent moved to dismiss under section 2-619(a)(9), relying on the release. (Def.’s Mot. Dismiss 3–5.) Raman responded that the release did not reach the gym’s failure to maintain its equipment and could not bar Count II. (Pl.’s Resp. to Def.’s Mot. Dismiss 4–9.) After a hearing, the court found the release “broad enough to cover any fall” and dismissed both counts with prejudice. (R. 22; C. 141.)

STANDARD OF REVIEW

A motion under section 2-619 admits the legal sufficiency of the complaint but raises an affirmative matter that defeats the claim. Doe v. Lakeview Academy, 2019 IL 124321, ¶ 14. This Court reviews a dismissal under section 2-619 de novo. Id. ¶ 15. Whether a release bars a claim is a question of contract interpretation, which is also reviewed de novo. Hendricks v. Lakeshore Fitness Club, Inc., 2018 IL App (1st) 171234, ¶ 21, aff’d, 2019 IL 123987.

ARGUMENT

The release bars neither count. It does not reach the gym’s failure to maintain its equipment, and no release can bar a claim for willful and wanton conduct.

I. The release does not reach Summit Ascent’s failure to maintain its auto-belay device.

An exculpatory clause is not favored and is strictly construed against the party it benefits. Harris v. Walker, 119 Ill. 2d 542, 548 (1988). It must spell out the parties’ intent with such clarity that the plaintiff knew the range of dangers she was assuming. Hendricks, 2018 IL App (1st) 171234, ¶ 24. The Restatement likewise reads a release of negligence against the party it protects. Restatement (Second) of Torts § 496B cmt. d (Am. L. Inst. 1965).

In Hendricks, a fitness club’s release covered injuries “arising from the use of club facilities,” yet it did not reach a member’s injury from a treadmill the club knew was broken. Hendricks, 2018 IL App (1st) 171234, ¶¶ 26–28. Other courts agree. Accord Garrison v. Ridgecrest Climbing Ctr., 2020-Ohio-4567, ¶ 19 (10th Dist.) (refusing to apply a climbing gym’s release to its failure to maintain belay equipment).

Here, the release speaks only of “the inherent risks of climbing, including falls.” (Compl. Ex. A, at 2.) A frayed cable that no one inspected for eleven weeks is not an inherent risk of climbing; it is the very hazard the auto-belay device exists to remove. Like the treadmill in Hendricks, the device failed because the gym did not maintain it. Raman could not have known that she was giving up a claim for the gym’s failure to inspect its own safety equipment.

Summit Ascent argued below that every fall is a risk of climbing. (Def.’s Mot. Dismiss 4.) But the release names falls as a risk of the sport, not falls caused by the gym’s neglect, and any doubt is resolved against the gym. See Harris, 119 Ill. 2d at 548. The release therefore does not bar Count I.

II. No release can bar a claim for willful and wanton conduct.

Illinois public policy forbids enforcing an exculpatory clause against a claim of willful and wanton conduct. Doe, 2019 IL 124321, ¶ 30; see also Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 195(1) (Am. L. Inst. 1981) (a term exempting a party from liability for harm caused intentionally or recklessly is unenforceable). Conduct is willful and wanton when it shows an utter indifference to or conscious disregard for the safety of others. 745 ILCS 10/1-210 (West 2022).

Here, the complaint alleges that the manager told staff to skip the daily checks to save time, knowing that the cable carried each climber’s full weight. (Compl. ¶¶ 16–18; Ortiz Dep. 31:4-19.) If proved, that is a conscious disregard for climbers’ safety.

A motion must also state each ground on which it rests. Cook Cnty. Cir. Ct. R. 2.1(c) (eff. Jan. 1, 2017). Summit Ascent’s motion gave no ground for dismissing Count II apart from the release. (Def.’s Mot. Dismiss 3–5.) An appellee who does not argue a point in its brief forfeits it. Ill. S. Ct. R. 341(h)(7) (eff. Oct. 1, 2020). The circuit court therefore erred in dismissing Count II.

CONCLUSION

For these reasons, Raman asks this Court to reverse the order dismissing her complaint and to remand for further proceedings.
